blocks.text: A **binary tree** is a set of **nodes** connected like an upside-down tree. Each node holds a **value** and points to at most **two children**: a **left** child and a **right** child. One node sits at the very top with no parent — the **root** — and every other node can be reached from it by following child links downward.

blocks.alt: A binary tree with root 1. Its children are 2 (left) and 3 (right). 2 has children 4 and 5; 3 has a right child 6. Nodes 4, 5 and 6 have no children and are leaves. The nodes 2, 4 and 5 together form the left subtree of 1.

blocks.text: Think of a family tree — upside down

Computer scientists draw trees with the root at the **top** and the branches growing **down**. The words come from family trees: a node's **children** are the nodes directly below it, its **parent** is the node directly above it, and two nodes with the same parent are **siblings**. "Binary" just means *at most two* children per node.

The most important idea in this whole course is hidden in the picture above: **every child is the root of a smaller tree of its own**. Node 2, with 4 and 5 under it, is a complete binary tree by itself — the **left subtree** of 1. That's why tree problems are solved with recursion: solve it for the two smaller trees, then combine.

blocks.alt: Depth, level and height on the example tree. The root 1 has depth 0. 2 and 3 have depth 1. 4, 5 and 6 have depth 2. The height of the tree is 2, the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

items: **Node** — one box in the tree: a value plus links to its children.
**Root** — the top node; the only node with no parent.
**Parent / child** — a link goes from a parent down to a child. Every node except the root has exactly one parent.
**Siblings** — two children of the same parent.
**Leaf** — a node with no children. **Internal node** — a node with at least one child.
**Edge** — the link between a parent and a child. A tree with n nodes has exactly **n − 1 edges**.
**Subtree** — a node together with everything below it.
**Depth of a node** — how many edges from the root down to it (the root has depth 0). Nodes with the same depth form a **level**.

**Height of a tree** — the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. (Some books count nodes instead of edges, so a one-node tree has height 1. LeetCode's "maximum depth" counts nodes.)
**Ancestor / descendant** — any node on the path up to the root is an ancestor; everything in a node's subtree is a descendant.

blocks.text: A tree node is a small class: a value and two child references, each either another node or null. This is exactly how LeetCode defines it:
Building the tree from the picture by hand means creating six nodes and wiring up their children:

blocks.code:
root = TreeNode(1)
root.left = TreeNode(2)
root.right = TreeNode(3)
root.left.left = TreeNode(4)
root.left.right = TreeNode(5)
root.right.right = TreeNode(6)   # 3 has no left child

blocks.text: How LeetCode writes a tree: one array, level by level

Interview questions give you a tree as an array like `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6]`. Read it **level by level, left to right**: the root first, then its two children, then their children, and so on. A `null` marks a missing child, so the positions still line up. Trailing nulls are dropped.

blocks.alt: The array 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6 coloured by level: 1 is level 0; 2 and 3 are level 1; 4, 5, null and 6 are level 2. The null is the missing left child of 3.

blocks.text: Turning the array back into nodes uses a **queue**: each node waits in line until the next two array slots become its children.

blocks.caption: Try the lopsided example: each null still uses up a slot.

blocks.code:
from collections import deque

def build_tree(values):
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    queue = deque([root])                 # nodes still waiting for children
    i = 1
    while queue and i < len(values):
        node = queue.popleft()
        if values[i] is not None:
            node.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:
            node.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root

blocks.text: Binary tree vs the structures you know

blocks.alt: An array is a row of slots reached by index. A linked list is a chain where each node points to one next node. A binary tree is a branching structure where each node points to up to two children.

blocks.text: A linked list is really a tree where every node has **one** child. Add a second child pointer and the chain starts to **branch** — and branching is what lets a tree reach a million items in about 20 steps, as the next lesson shows.

items: A binary tree is a **root** plus nodes that each have at most **two children**, left and right.
Every child is the root of its own **subtree** — the reason tree code is recursive.
**Depth** counts edges down from the root; **height** is the longest root-to-leaf path. A tree with n nodes has **n − 1 edges**.
LeetCode lists a tree **level by level**, with **null** for a missing child; a queue turns that array back into nodes.
